unique_rules_verified.name: AFDX frame structure without fragmentation
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule claims that AFDX frames 'shall not be fragmented' but this constraint is not explicitly stated in the provided specification text. While section 3.4.1.2 discusses 'Structure of an AFDX Frame Without Fragmentation' and shows frame structure diagrams, it does not contain a prohibition against fragmentation. The section title implies fragmentation is possible (by specifically addressing the case 'without fragmentation'), but no behavioral rule is stated that frames 'shall not be fragmented'.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: 3.4.1.2 Structure of an AFDX Frame Without Fragmentation - Figure 3-31 illustrates the structure of an AFDX frame. Minimum and maximum frames are illustrated

unique_rules_verified.name: IP source address format
unique_rules_verified.justification: The provided specification text does not contain any section 3.4.1.4.1 or any discussion of IP source address requirements. The text focuses on MAC addressing format, redundancy concepts, and integrity checking, but does not mention IP source address validation or IPv4 address requirements for transmitting End Systems.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: No relevant quote found - the specification text provided does not contain the claimed section 3.4.1.4.1 'IP Source Address' or any statements about IP source address format requirements.

unique_rules_verified.name: IP destination address format
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule claims to specify the format of IP destination addresses and references section '3.4.1.4.2 IP Destination Address', but this section does not exist in the provided specification text. The specification text covers sequence numbers, integrity checking, and redundancy management (sections 3.2.6.x), but does not contain any content about IP addressing formats or destination address requirements. The quoted rule text 'The IP destination address shall be a valid IPv4 address assigned to the receiving End System or a multicast group' is not found anywhere in the provided specification.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: No matching text found in the provided specification. The specification covers sequence numbers and integrity checking in sections 3.2.6.x, not IP addressing.

unique_rules_verified.name: Static Transmit Table Configuration
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule accurately describes the static configuration requirement for transmit table entries. The specification clearly shows a transmit table structure with all the specified fields (Src AFDX Communication Port, Src partition, Src UDP, Src IP, Src MAC, Dest UDP, Dest IP, Dest MAC) and indicates this is for VL identification.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The following tables show the address tables for each ES: Transmit Table of End-System 1: Src AFDX Communication Port, Src partition, Src UDP, Src IP, Src MAC, Dest UDP, Dest IP, Dest MAC

unique_rules_verified.name: Static Receive Table Configuration
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is genuinely stated in the specification. The receive table examples on page 47 clearly show that each entry must define all the specified fields: destination AFDX port(s), destination partition(s), source UDP port, source IP, source MAC, destination UDP port, destination IP, and destination MAC (with VL identification). The table headers and entries demonstrate this static configuration requirement.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Receive Table of End-System 2: Dest AFXD Communication Port(s) Dest partition(s) Src UDP Src IP Src MAC Dest UDP Dest IP Dest MAC AFDX Port 1 Partition 1 UDP1 IP10 MAC10 UDP1 IP1 MAC1 (VL1)

unique_rules_verified.name: Receiver Demultiplexing Based on Address Fields
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is explicitly stated in the specification. The COMMENTARY section on page 47 clearly states 'At the receiver, the demultiplexing is based only on the MAC, IP, UDP destination address.' This directly confirms that demultiplexing uses exactly the three address fields listed in the rule: MAC destination, IP destination, and UDP destination port.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: At the receiver, the demultiplexing is based only on the MAC, IP, UDP destination address.

unique_rules_verified.name: Unique Message Identification Quintuplet
unique_rules_verified.justification: This rule accurately captures the message identification quintuplet described in the specification. The source quote directly states that peer-to-peer communications are identified by the combination of UDP Source Port + Source IP + Destination MAC (VL identification) + Destination IP + UDP Destination Port. The extracted field values correctly list these five components that together form the unique identification quintuplet.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Peer-to-peer communications are identified in each frame by UDP Source Port + Source IP + Destination MAC (VL identification) + Destination IP + UDP Destination Port as illustrated in Figure 3-34.

unique_rules_verified.name: Unique Quintuplet per Message
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is explicitly stated in the specification. The text clearly states that 'Peer-to-peer communications are identified in each frame by UDP Source Port + Source IP + Destination MAC (VL identification) + Destination IP + UDP Destination Port' and that 'In the AFDX network, this quintuplet provides a unique identification for each message.' The specification also provides concrete examples showing how different messages are uniquely identified by their distinct quintuplets.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Peer-to-peer communications are identified in each frame by UDP Source Port + Source IP + Destination MAC (VL identification) + Destination IP + UDP Destination Port... In the AFDX network, this quintuplet provides a unique identification for each message.

unique_rules_verified.name: Static Quintuplet for Unidirectional Extra-AFDX Communication
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is directly supported by the specification text. Section 3.4.1.3.2 explicitly states that for unidirectional Extra-AFDX communication, 'the ES configuration table will contain the destination IP and port number. Hence there will be a statically defined quintuplet for addressing.' This confirms that the quintuplet must be statically defined in the configuration table for unidirectional Extra-AFDX communication.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The implication is that the ES configuration table will contain the destination IP and port number. Hence there will be a statically defined quintuplet for addressing.

unique_rules_verified.name: IP_Unicast_Address_Structure
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is genuine but has an error in the User_Defined_ID field size. According to Figure 3-36, the structure is: 1-bit Private IP address ('0'), 7-bits constant ('0001010'), 16-bits User_Defined_ID, then within the remaining bits: 13-bits for actual partition data and 3-bits Spare field. The original rule incorrectly shows User_Defined_ID as 16 bits and Partition_ID as 16 bits, but the specification clearly shows User_Defined_ID is 16 bits total, and the remaining partition-related bits are split between actual partition data (13 bits) and spare field (3 bits).
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: IP Unicast Addressing Format (source or unicast destination) 32-bits Class A 1-bit Private IP address 7-bits User_Defined_ID 16-bits Partition ID '0' '0001010' 'nnnn nnnn nnnn nnnn' Spare field 3-bits 5-bits

unique_rules_verified.name: IP_Unicast_Spare_Field_Usage
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is explicitly stated in the specification. The text clearly states 'The Spare field is normally not used and set to zero as shown in Figure 3-37.' Additionally, Figure 3-37 shows the Spare Field Meaning with '0 0 0' having 'No significance', confirming that the spare field should be set to zero (value 0).
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The Spare field is normally not used and set to zero as shown in Figure 3-37.

unique_rules_verified.name: IP_Multicast_Address_Structure
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is genuine and based on Figure 3-38 in the specification. However, the constant field value in the original rule appears to have a formatting issue. The specification shows '0000 1110 0000' which equals '000011100000' when spaces are removed, matching the corrected value. The structure and bit allocations are correct: 4 bits for Class D '1110', 12 bits for constant field '000011100000', and 16 bits for Virtual Link Identifier.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: IP Addressing Format 32 bits 4 bits 28 bits Class D "1110" IP Multicast Identifier Constant field 12 bits = "0000 1110 0000" Virtual Link Identifier 16 bits Figure 3-38 - IP Multicast Addressing Format

The rule appears to be an inference or generalization rather than a specific requirement stated in the specification.

unique_rules_verified.name: Memory to Medium Mapping for Integers

The rule correctly states that higher bit numbers and bytes are stored at lower memory addresses and transmitted first on the medium, which directly matches the specification's definition.

This is a fundamental requirement for data interoperability across different processor architectures.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: These data types have a well-defined bit and byte order that enables applications to send and receive a data element via the network regardless of the native bit or byte order of the host processors used in the system.

The rule also correctly identifies that these encoded values must map to valid abstract syntax values, which is implied by the transfer syntax concept - the encoding must represent valid enumerated labels as shown in Figure 1-1.1.

unique_rules_verified.name: 32-bit floating point formula (de-normalized)

However, the extracted formula uses 'x' as the multiplication operator while the specification uses 'x'. Both are mathematically equivalent, but for exact adherence to the specification text, the 'x' should be preserved.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The real number value for de-normalized numbers is given by the formula: (-1)^S x (0.F) x 2^E

unique_rules_verified.name: 64-bit floating point formula (normalized)
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is incorrect. While the specification does mention formulas for floating point representation, the specific formula referenced is for 32-bit floating point (Float_32), not 64-bit floating point (Float_64). unique_rules_verified.name: BAG value constraints
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is explicitly stated in the specification. This gives exactly the values [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128] ms. The commentary also confirms that BAG values are limited to powers of 2 to simplify ES design and that 128 ms is the maximum value used.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The Traffic shaping function of the ES should be able to handle BAG values in range 1 ms to 128 ms. These values should satisfy the following formula: BAG=2k [in ms], (k integer in range 0 to 7)... BAG values are limited to powers of 2 in order to simplify the ES design. If a partition needs to transmit data less often than 128 ms, the BAG value 128 will be used.

unique_rules_verified.name: Maximum Latency Calculation
unique_rules_verified.justification: This rule is directly stated in the specification. The text explicitly explains that in AFDX networks with bounded arrival distribution and exact bandwidth regulated traffic control, 'This results in a calculable maximum latency in the network, rather than a probabilistic latency.' This is contrasted with typical Ethernet networks that have probabilistic latency. The rule correctly captures this fundamental characteristic of AFDX.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: In an AFDX network, the analysis also assumes that the transmitting end-systems are not synchronized, but that frame delivery follows a bounded arrival distribution. This bounded arrival implies exact bandwidth regulated traffic control. Therefore, the distribution of latency on each connection through the network follows a distribution, which is bounded. This results in a calculable maximum latency in the network, rather than a probabilistic latency.

The text clearly defines Ji,switch as 'The Jitter (representing the Window a frame is assured to be located within) associated to VLi entering a particular switch' and explicitly states it is 'expressed in seconds'. The extracted rule accurately captures this definition and constraint.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The Jitter (representing the Window a frame is assured to be located within) associated to VLi entering a particular switch is Ji,switch (expressed in seconds)

unique_rules_verified.name: Default Reception VL Identifier Format
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule accurately captures the VL identifier format for default reception VLs as explicitly stated in the specification. The text clearly states that switches subscribe to 'VL (0, position)' where '0' indicates reception VL and 'position' depends on the switch's location in the aircraft network.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Depending of its position in the aircraft network, acquired by pin programming, the Switch subscribes by default to one unique reception VL, further called VL (0, position). Justification of the name VL (0, position): • '0' indicates that it is a reception VL • 'Position' to indicate that this VL depends on the position of the Switch in the aircraft

unique_rules_verified.name: Default Reception VL Non-Volatile Configuration
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is directly and explicitly stated in the specification. Section 4.7.2.2 clearly lists the exact three requirements that must be contained in non-volatile memory for the default reception VL configuration: VL identifiers (MAC destination address), Maximum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (smax), and Bandwidth Allocation Gap.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The reception part of the Default_Configuration_Table of the Switch should contain at least, in nonvolatile memory, the following information (characteristics of the default reception VL): • VL identifiers (MAC destination address): VL (0,position) • Maximum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (smax) • Bandwidth Allocation Gap

unique_rules_verified.name: Default Transmission VL Identifier Bit Mapping
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule accurately captures the pin programming specification for VL identifier bits P1 to P12. The specification clearly states that these bits correspond to pin programming values where '1 = GROUND and 0 = OPEN', which matches exactly with the extracted rule's constraint mapping.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Where P1 to P12 correspond to the following pin programming values: 1 = GROUND and 0 = OPEN.

unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The reception part of the Default_Configuration_Table of the Switch should contain at least, in nonvolatile memory, the following information (characteristics of the default reception VL): • VL identifiers (MAC destination address): VL (0,position) • Maximum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (smax) • Bandwidth Allocation Gap

unique_rules_verified.name: UDP port unreachable message prohibition
unique_rules_verified.justification: This rule is correctly extracted from the specification. The table explicitly states that UDP SHOULD send an ICMP Port Unreachable message for datagrams to ports with no pending LISTEN call, but AFDX marks this as 'NOT APPLICABLE' with the comment 'Only ICMP echo request and echo reply are allowed.' This effectively prohibits ICMP Port Unreachable messages in AFDX implementations.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: If a datagram arrives addressed to a UDP port for which there is no pending LISTEN call, UDP SHOULD send an ICMP Port Unreachable message. [AFDX: NOT APPLICABLE - Only ICMP "echo request" and "echo reply" are allowed.]

unique_rules_verified.name: Virtual Link Bandwidth and Frame Interval Bounds
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule accurately captures a fundamental requirement stated in the specification. The text explicitly states 'This is achieved by bounding both the bandwidth and the frame delivery interval for each VL.' This describes the exact behavioral constraint that Virtual Links must have bounded bandwidth and frame delivery intervals to maintain deterministic network properties.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: This is achieved by bounding both the bandwidth and the frame delivery interval for each VL.

unique_rules_verified.name: Single source per VL constraint
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is explicitly stated in the specification. The text clearly states that only one End System within the Avionics network should be the source of any one VL, which directly supports the extracted rule about single source per VL constraint.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Only one End System within the Avionics network should be the source of any one VL.

unique_rules_verified.name: Switch subscribes to unique default reception VL
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is directly stated in the specification. Section 4.7.2.2 explicitly states that 'Depending of its position in the aircraft network, acquired by pin programming, the Switch subscribes by default to one unique reception VL, further called VL (0, position).' The word 'unique' and 'one' confirm that each switch subscribes to exactly one reception VL based on its position.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Depending of its position in the aircraft network, acquired by pin programming, the Switch subscribes by default to one unique reception VL, further called VL (0, position).

unique_rules_verified.source_quote: Each Switch has a unique default transmission VL, further called VL (1, position).

unique_rules_verified.name: Maximum allowed total Ethernet line size per VL
unique_rules_verified.justification: The specification clearly states that both default reception and transmission VL configurations must contain 'Maximum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (smax)' as a configurable parameter. unique_rules_verified.source_quote: The reception part of the Default_Configuration_Table of the Switch should contain at least, in nonvolatile memory, the following information (characteristics of the default reception VL): • VL identifiers (MAC destination address): VL (0,position) • Maximum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (smax) • Bandwidth Allocation Gap

unique_rules_verified.name: Minimum allowed total Ethernet line size per VL

unique_rules_verified.source_quote: On a per VL basis: ... • Minimum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (Smin)

unique_rules_verified.name: VL priority classification
unique_rules_verified.justification: The rule is explicitly stated in the specification text. Under section 4.7.3.2 Filtering_Policing and_Forwarding_Configuration_Table, it clearly lists 'Prioritization (high or low)' as one of the parameters required on a per VL basis. This confirms that VL priority can only be classified as either 'high' or 'low'.
unique_rules_verified.source_quote: On a per VL basis: • Input physical port • List of output physical ports • MAC destination address (VL identifier VLi) • Bandwith Allocation Gap (BAGi) • Maximum allowed Jitter • ACcount (ACi) [specifying if this account is shared or not] • Maximum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (Smax) • Minimum allowed Total Ethernet Line size (Smin) • Prioritization (high or low)
